def-res-cooks.title: Cook’s distance, DFFITS, DFBETAS
def-res-cooks.html:
Let hii<1, and let cjj be the jth diagonal entry of (X⊤X)−1, so that s2cjj is the estimated variance of β^j.

  1. Cook’s distance is 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃Di=(β^(i)−β^)⊤X⊤X(β^(i)−β^)ps2.

  2. DFFITS is the change in case i’s own fitted value in units of its standard error, 𝛃DFFITSi=y^i−x(i)⊤β^(i)s(i)hii.

  3. DFBETAS is the change in one coefficient in units of its standard error, DFBETASij=β^j−β^j(i)s(i)cjj.

  4. COVRATIO compares the generalized variances of the estimates with and without case i, COVRATIOi=det(s(i)2(X(i)⊤X(i))−1)det(s2(X⊤X)−1).

def-res-lts.title: Least trimmed squares
def-res-lts.html: Let q be an integer with n/2≤q≤n. For b∈Rp, let r[1]2(b)≤⋯≤r[n]2(b) be the ordered squared residuals (yi−x(i)⊤b)2. The least trimmed squares (LTS) estimate minimizes T(b)=∑k=1qr[k]2(b), the sum of the q smallest squared residuals. The least median of squares (LMS) estimate minimizes r[⌈n/2⌉]2(b) instead.

def-res-m-estimator.title: M-estimator of regression
def-res-m-estimator.html:
Let ρ:R→[0,∞) be even, nondecreasing on [0,∞), differentiable, with ρ(0)=0, and put ψ=ρ′ and w(u)=ψ(u)/u (with w(0)=limu→0ψ(u)/u). Given a scale σ^>0, an M-estimate 𝛃β^M minimizes Q(b)=∑i=1nρ(yi−x(i)⊤bσ^). Two choices of ρ are standard.

  1. Huber: ρ(u)=u2/2 for |u|≤k and k|u|−k2/2 beyond, so ψ(u)=max(−k,min(k,u)) and w(u)=min(1,k/|u|).

  2. Bisquare (Tukey’s biweight): ρ(u)=c26[1−(1−u2/c2)3] for |u|≤c and c2/6 beyond, so ψ(u)=u(1−u2/c2)2 and w(u)=(1−u2/c2)2 for |u|<c, and ψ(u)=w(u)=0 beyond.

def-res-partial-leverage.title: Partial leverage
def-res-partial-leverage.html: The partial leverage of case i for the coefficient of xj is ℓij=x~ij2‖x~j‖2.

def-res-residuals.title: Standardized and studentized residuals
def-res-residuals.html:
Let hii<1. For case i:

  1. the raw residual is 𝛃ε^i=yi−x(i)⊤β^;

  2. the standardized residual is zi=ε^i/(σ1−hii), which needs the true σ;

  3. the internally studentized residual is ri=ε^is1−hii;

  4. the externally studentized residual is ti=ε^is(i)1−hii, where s(i)2=SSE(i)/(n−p−1) is the residual mean square of the least squares fit to the n−1 cases other than i.

eq-res-cluster-solve.html: (X⊤X)−1x⋆=A−1x⋆1+mh⋆.

eq-res-m-equations.html: ∑i=1nψ(yi−x(i)⊤bσ^)x(i)=0⟺X⊤W(b)(y−Xb)=0,

eq-res-mean-shift.html: 𝛃𝛆𝛆Y=Xβ+Δei+ε,ε∼Nn(0,σ2I),

eq-res-press.html: PRESS=∑i=1n(ε^i1−hii)2,

eq-res-residual-error.html: 𝛆𝛆ε^=(I−M)ε,

eq-res-residual-moments.html: Corr(ε^i,ε^j)=−hij(1−hii)(1−hjj).

exm-res-curvature.title: Curvature seen two ways
exm-res-curvature.html: In 120 simulated cases, x1 is uniform on (0,4), x2 is correlated with it (sample correlation 0.87), and E(Y)=1+x2+0.7(x1−2)2. The fitted model is linear in both, with coefficient −0.144 for x1, the slope of both panels of Figure 20.1.2. A quadratic fitted to the component-plus-residual plot (b) has leading coefficient 0.671, close to the true 0.7. In the added-variable plot (a) the curve is smeared, because its horizontal axis mixes x1 with x2, and the corresponding coefficient is 0.309.

exm-res-dc-outlier.title: Is the District of Columbia an outlier?
exm-res-dc-outlier.title_html: Is the District of Columbia an outlier?
exm-res-dc-outlier.html:
For the murder-rate regression with all 51 jurisdictions, the District of Columbia has raw residual 4.475, leverage 0.506, ri=3.658 and ti=4.278 (as in @exm-cmp-dc); deleting it lowers s=1.741 to s(i)=1.489. Its single-case p-value is 9.4×10−5, and the Bonferroni-adjusted value 0.0048 (critical value 3.522). The next case, Mississippi, has ti=−2.877 and adjusted p-value 0.310. Among the 50 states alone the most extreme is Louisiana, ti=3.299, adjusted p-value 0.095; such sequential testing is not covered by @thm-res-external-t(d), and Section 20.5 shows it can fail badly.

The test says that the District’s murder rate is incompatible with the linear relation that holds for the states. It does not say the number is wrong or that the case should be dropped. The District is a city, with regressors outside the range of the states; a defensible analysis restricts the population to states and says so.

exm-res-engel-leverage.title: Leverage in Engel’s household budgets
exm-res-engel-leverage.html: Engel’s 1857 survey records the annual income and food expenditure of 235 Belgian working-class households. Income is strongly skewed (skewness 2.78): the median is 884 and the largest, row 138 of the file, is 4958. In the straight-line regression of food expenditure on income the average leverage is 2/235=0.0085, and the richest household has leverage 0.255, about 30 times the average; the next largest is 0.058. Since hii−1/n=(xi−x¯)2/Sxx, this one household supplies a quarter (0.251) of the spread of income about its mean, and the fitted line will pass near it whatever it spends on food. On the logarithmic scale its leverage is 0.070, still the largest but no longer in a class of its own. Choosing the scale (Chapter 22) decides which cases the fit depends on.

exm-res-engel-robust.title: Engel’s budgets, robustly
exm-res-engel-robust.html:
For food expenditure on income in Engel’s data (@exm-res-engel-leverage), least squares gives slope 0.485, Huber 0.537 and bisquare 0.553. The bisquare fit gives weight zero to 3 households, rows 59,105,138 (Figure 20.6.1(b)). Row 138, the case of highest leverage (income 4958, food 1827, far below the line through the others, Huber weight 0.117), pulls the least squares slope down; in the least squares fit its externally studentized residual is −8.39 and its Cook’s distance 9.28.

But the spread of food expenditure grows with income. On the logarithmic scale the three fits nearly agree (slopes 0.856, 0.868, 0.871) and the smallest bisquare weight is 0.16: nobody is rejected. The robust fit correctly reported that a few cases disagree with a constant-variance line; whether the data or the scale is wrong no fit can decide (Chapter 21, Chapter 22).

exm-res-masking.title: Four identical bad records
exm-res-masking.html:
Thirty clean cases have x uniform on (0,10) and y=2+0.5x+ε, σ=0.5. Four identical records are added at x=20, y=2, where the clean line predicts about 12 (Figure 20.5.1(a)). The slope drops from 0.514 (clean cases) to 0.007, and s rises from 0.608 to 1.632. Here h⋆=1.126 (it can exceed one, since x=20 is outside the clean design, as in @prp-ci-new-leverage) and δ=−10.150. Each bad case has leverage 0.205, below 1/m=0.25, where a single copy would have 0.530; residual −1.844; prediction residual −2.318; and ti=−1.28. Deleting the group changes 𝛃β^ 17.51 times as much as deleting one member.

The single-case diagnostics fail as predicted. The Bonferroni test (critical value 3.49) flags nothing, and the only case with |ti|>2 is a clean one: case 30, the clean case with largest x (9.86), has ti=2.25, because the dragged line passes below it. Cook’s distance does a little better: each bad case has Di=0.206, above 4/n=0.118 (no clean case exceeds it; the largest is 0.100) but far below the median of F(2,32). A single bad record alone would have had ti=−11.45 and Di=13.46. Deleting the four together tells the truth: their prediction residuals are all δ, and @thm-res-group-deletion(d) gives F=50.6 on 4 and 28 degrees of freedom, p-value 2.0×10−12. The difficulty is not in testing the cluster but in finding it.

exm-res-patterns.title: Four residual plots
exm-res-patterns.html: Each panel of Figure 20.1.1 comes from 80 simulated cases with x uniform on (0,10), fitted by a straight line. In (a) the model is right and the residuals form a structureless band. In (b) the mean has a quadratic term, and the residuals show the parabola the line could not absorb. In (c) the error standard deviation grows with x, and the band opens into a fan. In (d) one response has an error of 8σ; it stands out, and the line has been pulled slightly towards it. In every panel the residuals are orthogonal to the fitted values, as @prp-res-plots(a) requires; the listing prints the inner product.

exm-res-robust-masking.title: Robust fits on the masking data
exm-res-robust-masking.title_html: Robust fits on the masking data
exm-res-robust-masking.html: For the data of @exm-res-masking (Figure 20.6.1(a)), least squares has slope 0.007, and the Huber fit 0.005, with Huber weight 1.000 for each bad record: they have captured the fit so completely that their residuals are not even downweighted. The bisquare fit started from least squares is captured too (slope 0.005). LTS with q=18 of the 34 cases has slope 0.546 and robust scale 0.587; in that scale each bad record has standardized residual −18.6, and no clean case exceeds 2.81. The bisquare fit started from LTS has slope 0.509 and intercept 1.930, close to the clean fit (0.514 and 1.862), and gives the four records weight zero.

exm-res-state-influence.title: How much does the District of Columbia matter?
exm-res-state-influence.title_html: How much does the District of Columbia matter?
exm-res-state-influence.html:
In the murder-rate regression with all 51 jurisdictions, the District of Columbia has Di=3.430, seven times the next largest (Mississippi, 0.481); the median of F(4,47) is 0.851, and deleting the District moves 𝛃β^ to the boundary of the 0.985 confidence ellipsoid. Its DFFITS is 4.333 (cut-off 0.560) and its DFBETAS for poverty −1.090 (cut-off 0.280). Its partial leverage for poverty is only 0.032 (@exm-res-state-partial), but by @thm-res-influence(c) it is multiplied by ti2/(1−hii): 4.2782×0.032/(1−0.506)≈1.19, so |DFBETAS|≈1.09. Alaska, with the largest partial leverage (0.141), has ti=−0.760 and DFBETAS 0.315.

The consequences are substantive. With the District, the poverty coefficient is 0.1551 (standard error 0.1059, t=1.47); without it, 0.2538 (standard error 0.0934, t=2.72), the fit of @exm-proj-fwl-crime. One jurisdiction decides whether poverty has a detectable association with murder rates given the other regressors, and the single-parent coefficient moves from 0.6256 to 0.3980. The cut-offs flag 2 cases by Di>4/n=0.078, 3 by DFFITS, 5 by DFBETAS for poverty and 4 by leverage above 2p/n=0.157, but only the District changes a conclusion. Its COVRATIO is 0.578: it inflates the estimated generalized variance through its contribution to s2.

exm-res-state-partial.title: Where the District of Columbia’s leverage comes from
exm-res-state-partial.title_html: Where the District of Columbia’s leverage comes from
exm-res-state-partial.html: In the murder-rate regression for the 51 jurisdictions, with poverty, single-parent households and urbanization as regressors, the District of Columbia has leverage 0.506 (@exm-proj-leverage) but partial leverage for poverty only 0.032: its leverage comes from its extreme single-parent and urban percentages, not from its poverty rate. The largest partial leverage for poverty is Alaska’s, 0.141. Section 20.4 shows that the District nevertheless moves the poverty coefficient more than any other case, because influence also depends on the residual.

exr-res-affine-invariance.title: A2
exr-res-affine-invariance.html: Show that with an intercept the leverages are unchanged when the regressors are replaced by a+Bx with B nonsingular, but not under a nonlinear transformation (@exm-res-engel-leverage). Use @prp-proj-leverage-mahalanobis.

exr-res-catcher.title: B1
exr-res-catcher.html: Let C=(X⊤X)−1X⊤. Show that the sum of squares of the jth row of C is cjj, and deduce that ∑iℓij=1 in a second way. Why does this suggest a cut-off of order 1/n for DFBETAS?

exr-res-cook-hand.title: A1
exr-res-cook-hand.html: In a regression with p=3, case i has ri=2. Compute Di when hii=0.1 and when hii=0.6. Which case would you look at first, and why might neither be alarming?

exr-res-covratio.title: B3
exr-res-covratio.html: Use @thm-res-influence(e) to show that for large n and small p/n, COVRATIOi≈1+hii−p(ti2−1)/n. Deduce the cut-off |COVRATIOi−1|>3p/n from the two extreme cases hii≈0, |ti|=2 and hii=2p/n, ti=0.

exr-res-dc-conversion.title: A1
exr-res-dc-conversion.html: Use @thm-res-external-t(c) to compute the District of Columbia’s ti from its ri=3.658, with n=51 and p=4.

exr-res-deleted-variance.title: B2
exr-res-deleted-variance.html: Show that s(i)<s iff ri2>1. Interpret.

exr-res-direct-t.title: B1
exr-res-direct-t.html: Prove @thm-res-external-t(b) with Δ=0 directly. Show that 𝛃yi−x(i)⊤β^(i) is independent of s(i)2, that its variance is σ2(1+x(i)⊤(X(i)⊤X(i))−1x(i)), and that this equals σ2/(1−hii).

exr-res-equal-leverage.title: B2
exr-res-equal-leverage.html: Show that maxihii≥p/n, with equality iff all leverages equal p/n. Show that if X has orthogonal columns and every entry is ±1, then all leverages equal p/n.

exr-res-gaussian-rank.title: C1
exr-res-gaussian-rank.html: Complete the proof of @prp-res-leverage-beta by showing that if Z is n×k with independent N(0,1) entries and n≥k+2, then CZ has rank k with probability one. Hint: add columns one at a time, and use that a nonzero normal vector with a nonsingular covariance restricted to a subspace falls in a fixed proper subspace with probability zero.

exr-res-group-cook.title: C2
exr-res-group-cook.html: For a set D of cases, define 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃DD=(β^(D)−β^)⊤X⊤X(β^(D)−β^)/(ps2). Using @thm-res-group-deletion(b), show that 𝛆𝛆DD=ε^D⊤(I−HD)−1HD(I−HD)−1ε^D/(ps2).

exr-res-group-single.title: A2
exr-res-group-single.html: Show that @thm-res-group-deletion with D={i} gives parts (b), (d) and (e) of @thm-res-deletion, and that FD=ti2.

exr-res-half-leverage.title: A2
exr-res-half-leverage.html: A case has leverage 0.5 and residual 1. By how much does its own fitted value change when it is deleted, and what is its prediction residual? What is the prediction residual of a case with leverage 0.9 and the same raw residual?

exr-res-heavy-tails-outlier.title: C1
exr-res-heavy-tails-outlier.html: Suppose the errors are independent with a t distribution on 3 degrees of freedom and the design is that of the state data. By simulation, estimate the probability that the 5% Bonferroni outlier test rejects. Explain the result in terms of the warning at the end of this section.

exr-res-huber-breakdown.title: C1
exr-res-huber-breakdown.html: Consider regression through the origin, E(Y)=βx, and an M-estimate with fixed scale σ^=1 and a continuous, nondecreasing, bounded, odd ψ with ψ(u)>0 for u>0. Add to fixed data (xi,yi), i<n, one case (xn,yn)=(L,aL). Show that as L→∞ every solution β^L of ∑iψ(yi−β^xi)xi=0 tends to a. Conclude that the breakdown point is 1/n.

exr-res-huber-weights.title: A1
exr-res-huber-weights.html: With k=1.345, compute the Huber weights of standardized residuals 0.5, 2 and 10. With c=4.685, compute the bisquare weights of the same residuals.

exr-res-internal-correlation.title: C1
exr-res-internal-correlation.html: Assume @eq-opt-normal-model with n−p≥2 and leverages below one. Show that E(rirj)=−hij/(1−hii)(1−hjj) for i≠j. Hint: write ri=n−pui⊤W with 𝛆𝛆W=(I−M)ε/‖(I−M)ε‖, and show that E(WW⊤)=(I−M)/(n−p).

exr-res-leverage-limit.title: B1
exr-res-leverage-limit.html: In the setting of @prp-res-leverage-beta, show that n(hii−1/n) converges in law to χ2(k) as n→∞.

exr-res-ls-one-step.title: A2
exr-res-ls-one-step.html: Show that least squares is the M-estimator with ρ(u)=u2/2, that its weights are all one, and that IRLS started anywhere reaches it in one step.

exr-res-lts-starts.title: B2
exr-res-lts-starts.html: Find the smallest number N of elemental starts for which (1−(1−ϵ)p)N≤0.01 when ϵ=0.2 and p=4, and when ϵ=0.4 and p=10. What does the second answer say about high-breakdown fitting with many regressors?

exr-res-lts-subsets.title: B1
exr-res-lts-subsets.html: Show that minbT(b)=minHSSEH, where H ranges over the q-subsets of cases for which the rows of X in H have full column rank and SSEH is the residual sum of squares of least squares on H (assume at least one such subset exists). Deduce that an LTS estimate is the least squares estimate on some q-subset.

exr-res-masking-numbers.title: A1
exr-res-masking-numbers.html: Check the leverage 0.205 and the residual −1.844 in @exm-res-masking from h⋆=1.126, δ=−10.150 and m=4.

exr-res-misspecified-quadratic.title: B2
exr-res-misspecified-quadratic.html: Simple linear regression is fitted to xi=i, i=1,…,n, but E(Yi)=β0+β1xi+γxi2. Use @prp-res-plots(c) to show that the expected residuals lie on a parabola in i, and find its vertex.

exr-res-origin-leverage.title: A1
exr-res-origin-leverage.html: For regression through the origin on one regressor, show that hii=xi2/∑kxk2. Give data with n=10 in which one leverage exceeds 0.99.

exr-res-outlier-power.title: B3
exr-res-outlier-power.html: In the setting of @thm-res-external-t, the shift at case i is detected by the single-case test with probability Pr{|T|>c}, T∼t(n−p−1,Δ1−hii/σ). Show that for fixed Δ and c this probability decreases as hii increases. Hint: T2 has a noncentral F law; use @thm-qf-f-power.

exr-res-partial-cluster.title: B3
exr-res-partial-cluster.html: In the setting of @prp-res-masking, delete k<m of the cluster cases. Show that each deleted case has prediction residual δ/(1+(m−k)h⋆). What does this say about searching for a cluster of unknown size by deleting sets of size k?

exr-res-plot-omitted.title: B1
exr-res-plot-omitted.html: Let 1∈C(X), let z∉C(X) be a candidate regressor, let γ^ be its coefficient when it is added to the model, and let Rz2 be the R2 of the regression of z on X. Show that the least squares slope of the plot of 𝛆ε^ against z is γ^(1−Rz2). Why is the added-variable plot the better tool for judging whether z belongs in the model?

exr-res-quadratic-leverage.title: B3
exr-res-quadratic-leverage.html: Take x=−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3. Compute the leverage of the case at x=0 for the straight-line model and for the quadratic model E(Y)=β0+β1x+β2x2. Explain the difference.

exr-res-rank-one-inverse.title: B1
exr-res-rank-one-inverse.html: Show that for HD=h11⊤ (d×d) with dh≠1, (I−h11⊤)−1=I+h11⊤/(1−dh), and use it to recompute the group term 𝛆𝛆ε^D⊤(I−HD)−1ε^D in the proof of @prp-res-masking(e) from 𝛆ε^D=δ1/(1+mh⋆).

exr-res-robust-weights-plot.title: B3
exr-res-robust-weights-plot.html: For the state murder-rate regression with all 51 jurisdictions, fit Huber and bisquare M-estimates with statsmodels and list the jurisdictions with the smallest weights. Compare the poverty coefficient with the least squares values with and without the District of Columbia (@exm-res-state-influence).

exr-res-simple-dfbetas.title: B2
exr-res-simple-dfbetas.html: For simple regression, show that the DFBETAS of case i for the slope is ti(xi−x¯)/Sxx(1−hii). Which cases can change the slope most?

exr-res-small-df.title: A1
exr-res-small-df.html: A straight line is fitted to n=3 points. Show that every internally studentized residual satisfies |ri|=1 (unless all three residuals are zero), whatever the data. What does this say about using ri to judge a fit with one residual degree of freedom?

exr-res-swamping-sign.title: B2
exr-res-swamping-sign.html: In simple regression with clean mean x¯0 and S0=∑(xj−x¯0)2, show that hj⋆=1/n0+(xj−x¯0)(x⋆−x¯0)/S0. In @exm-res-masking, with x⋆ far to the right and δ<0, which clean residuals does @prp-res-masking(e) push up, and which down? Explain why case 30 was flagged.

exr-res-two-clusters.title: C1
exr-res-two-clusters.html: Place two clusters of m identical bad cases at the two ends of a straight-line design, one above the clean line and one below. Describe, using @thm-res-group-deletion, what single-case deletion, deletion of one cluster, and deletion of both clusters report. Is it possible for each cluster to mask the other?

exr-res-weighted-sum.title: A2
exr-res-weighted-sum.html: Show that ∑i(1−hii)ri2=n−p for any data. Deduce that if every leverage is at most hmax<1, then at most (n−p)/((1−hmax)c2) cases can have |ri|>c.

exr-res-zero-residual.title: A2
exr-res-zero-residual.html: Show that Di=0 iff ε^i=0, whatever the leverage. Give an example of a case with leverage 0.9 and no influence.

prp-res-cook-null.title: Cook’s distance under the model
prp-res-cook-null.html: Assume @eq-opt-normal-model with n−p≥2 and all leverages below one. Then Di=n−pphii1−hiiBi with Bi∼Beta(12,n−p−12), so E(Di)=hiip(1−hii),1n∑i=1nE(Di)≥1n−p, with equality in the last bound iff all leverages equal p/n.

prp-res-cstep.title: Concentration step
prp-res-cstep.html: Let b∈Rp, let H be a set of q cases with the smallest squared residuals at b, and suppose the rows of X in H have full column rank. Let b′ be the least squares estimate computed from the cases in H. Then T(b′)≤T(b).

prp-res-internal.title: Law of the internally studentized residual
prp-res-internal.title_html: Law of the internally studentized residual
prp-res-internal.html:
Assume @eq-opt-normal-model, n−p≥2 and hii<1. Then:

  1. ri2/(n−p)∼Beta(12,n−p−12);

  2. |ri|≤n−p, E(ri)=0 and Var(ri)=1;

  3. the law of ri is the same for every case and does not depend on X, 𝛃β or σ2.

prp-res-irls.title: IRLS descends
prp-res-irls.html: Suppose ρ(u)=g(u2), where g:[0,∞)→[0,∞) is concave, nondecreasing, and differentiable on (0,∞) with a finite limit g′(0+). Then w(u)=2g′(u2)≥0. Hold σ^ fixed, and suppose X⊤WX is nonsingular at every step. Then every IRLS step satisfies Q(b(t+1))≤Q(b(t)). The Huber and bisquare ρ satisfy the hypotheses.

prp-res-leverage-beta.title: Leverage under a Gaussian design
prp-res-leverage-beta.html: Let X=[1,Z], where the rows of the n×k matrix Z are independent 𝛍Nk(μ,Σ) vectors with Σ positive definite, and let n≥k+2. Then X has full column rank p=k+1 with probability one, and for every i, hii−1/n1−1/n∼Beta(k2,n−1−k2).

prp-res-masking.title: Masking and swamping by a cluster
prp-res-masking.title_html: Masking and swamping by a cluster
prp-res-masking.html:
Let X0 (n0×p, full column rank) and y0 be the clean cases, with least squares estimate 𝛃β^0, residuals 𝛃ε˘j=yj−x(j)⊤β^0 and residual sum of squares SSE0. Add m≥1 cases, each with row x⋆⊤ and response y⋆. Put A=X0⊤X0, 𝛃h⋆=x⋆⊤A−1x⋆,δ=y⋆−x⋆⊤β^0, the leverage of x⋆ relative to the clean design and the distance of the cluster from the clean fit. In the least squares fit to all n0+m cases:

  1. each cluster case has leverage h=h⋆/(1+mh⋆)<1/m;

  2. each cluster case has residual δ/(1+mh⋆);

  3. deleting one cluster case gives it prediction residual δ/(1+(m−1)h⋆) and changes the estimate by 𝛃𝛃β^−β^(i)=A−1x⋆δ/[(1+mh⋆)(1+(m−1)h⋆)];

  4. deleting the whole cluster gives each member prediction residual δ, and 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃β^−β^(D)=m(1+(m−1)h⋆)(β^−β^(i));

  5. clean case j has residual ε˘j−mδhj⋆/(1+mh⋆), where hj⋆=x(j)⊤A−1x⋆, and SSE=SSE0+mδ2/(1+mh⋆).

prp-res-max-leverage.title: Leverage vanishes in large samples
prp-res-max-leverage.html: Let the rows x(1),x(2),… be independent copies of a random vector x with E‖x‖2<∞ and E(xx⊤) positive definite, and let hii(n) be the leverages of the first n rows. Then maxi≤nhii(n)→0 in probability.

prp-res-partial-leverage.title: Properties of partial leverage
prp-res-partial-leverage.html:
Let hii(j) be the leverages of the model without xj. Then:

  1. hii=hii(j)+ℓij for every i;

  2. 0≤ℓij≤1 and ∑iℓij=1;

  3. ℓij is the leverage of case i in the regression through the origin of y~=(I−M(j))y on x~j, the regression drawn in the added-variable plot for xj;

  4. β^j=∑i(x~ij/‖x~j‖2)yi, so the weight of yi in β^j has square ℓij/‖x~j‖2=ℓijVar(β^j)/σ2.

prp-res-partial-residual.title: Two plots with the same line
prp-res-partial-residual.title_html: Two plots with the same line
prp-res-partial-residual.html:
Let 1∈C(X), and let xj be a column of X that is not a multiple of 1.

  1. The least squares line of 𝛆ε^+β^jxj on [1,xj] has intercept 0, slope β^j, and residual vector 𝛆ε^.

  2. The least squares line through the origin of y~ on x~j has slope β^j and residual vector 𝛆ε^.

prp-res-plots.title: What least squares leaves in the residuals
prp-res-plots.title_html: What least squares leaves in the residuals
prp-res-plots.html:
Suppose 1∈C(X).

  1. The residual vector is orthogonal to 1, to every column of X and to Y^. Hence the least squares line through a plot of the residuals against the fitted values, or against any regressor in the model, is the horizontal axis.

  2. The least squares line through a plot of the residuals against the responses yi has slope 1−R2.

  3. If in fact 𝛃𝛅E(Y)=Xβ+δ for some 𝛅δ∈Rn, and Cov(Y)=σ2I, then 𝛆𝛅E(ε^)=(I−M)δ and 𝛆Cov(ε^)=σ2(I−M).

prp-res-press.title: Expected PRESS
prp-res-press.html: Under the second-moment model of Section 20.1, E(PRESS)=σ2∑i=1n11−hii ≥ σ2n2n−p, with equality iff all leverages equal p/n. By comparison, the expected sum of squared errors in predicting new responses at the same n design points is σ2(n+p) (@prp-cor-optimism(a)), which is smaller than σ2n2/(n−p) by σ2p2/(n−p).

thm-res-deletion.title: Leave-one-out formulas
thm-res-deletion.html:
Let X have full column rank, and let X(i) be X without row i.

  1. X(i) has full column rank iff hii<1. Assume this from now on.

  2. 𝛃𝛃β^−β^(i)=(X⊤X)−1x(i)ε^i/(1−hii).

  3. Y^−Y^(i)=X(X⊤X)−1x(i)ε^i/(1−hii); that is, the fitted value of case j moves by hjiε^i/(1−hii). In particular case i’s own fitted value moves by hiiε^i/(1−hii).

  4. The prediction residual of case i is 𝛃yi−x(i)⊤β^(i)=ε^i/(1−hii).

  5. (n−p−1)s(i)2=(n−p)s2−ε^i2/(1−hii).

thm-res-external-t.title: Law of the externally studentized residual
thm-res-external-t.title_html: Law of the externally studentized residual
thm-res-external-t.html:
Assume @eq-res-mean-shift with hii<1 and n−p≥2.

  1. In the model with columns [X,ei], the least squares estimate of the shift is 𝛃Δ^=ε^i/(1−hii)=yi−x(i)⊤β^(i), the estimate of 𝛃β is 𝛃β^(i), the residual mean square is s(i)2, and the t statistic for Δ=0 is ti.

  2. ti∼t(n−p−1, Δ1−hii/σ). In particular, if Δ=0, then ti∼t(n−p−1).

  3. ti=ri(n−p−1)/(n−p−ri2), an increasing function of ri that maps (−n−p,n−p) onto the whole real line.

  4. (Bonferroni outlier test.) If no case is shifted, that is under @eq-opt-normal-model, and hjj<1 for every j, then Pr{maxj|tj|>tn−p−1,α/(2n)}≤α. Equivalently, the adjusted p-value min(1,np(1)), where p(1) is the smallest of the single-case two-sided p-values from (b), is valid.

thm-res-group-deletion.title: Deleting a set of cases
thm-res-group-deletion.html:
Let X and X(D) have full column rank. Then I−HD is nonsingular, and

  1. 𝛃𝛆yD−XDβ^(D)=(I−HD)−1ε^D;

  2. 𝛃𝛃𝛆β^−β^(D)=(X⊤X)−1XD⊤(I−HD)−1ε^D;

  3. 𝛆𝛆SSE(D)=SSE−ε^D⊤(I−HD)−1ε^D;

  4. if n−p−d≥1, then under @eq-opt-normal-model 𝛆𝛆FD=ε^D⊤(I−HD)−1ε^D/dSSE(D)/(n−p−d)∼F(d, n−p−d), and FD is the F statistic for 𝛄γ=0 in the mean-shift model 𝛃𝛄E(Y)=Xβ+EDγ.

thm-res-influence.title: Influence identities
thm-res-influence.html:
Let hii<1 and n−p≥2, and let x~j and ℓij be as in @def-res-partial-leverage.

  1. Di=‖Y^−Y^(i)‖2ps2=ri2p⋅hii1−hii.

  2. DFFITSi=tihii/(1−hii), and Di=DFFITSi2s(i)2/(ps2).

  3. DFBETASij=tix~ij‖x~j‖1−hii, so DFBETASij2=ti2ℓij/(1−hii).

  4. For every 𝛌λ≠0, 𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛌(λ⊤β^−λ⊤β^(i))2s(i)2λ⊤(X⊤X)−1λ≤DFFITSi2, with equality at 𝛌λ=x(i). In particular |DFBETASij|≤|DFFITSi| for every j.

  5. COVRATIOi=11−hii(n−pn−p−1+ti2)p.
